mappings.note: List objects around you and the material each is made of. Identifying materials from what you can see, LO-53; nothing is sorted into classes yet, so not LO-55.
What the grouping activity taught -- objects were grouped by a chosen property such as shape, colour, hardness or shine. Classifying on observable properties, LO-55.
Why cloth will not do for a water tumbler, and what would. The deliverable is a material choice for a purpose, LO-62.
Drop the balls and record which bounces highest. A conducted comparison with tabulated results, LO-56.
Fill the hard/soft table for brick, bottle, pillow, tumbler, table, sweater and compare with friends. Sorting by an observable property, LO-55.
Predict then observe whether sugar, salt, chalk, sand and sawdust disappear in water. LO-56 for the predict-and-test cycle, LO-55 because soluble/insoluble is one of its own named classes.
Weigh equal volumes of water, sand and pebbles and infer which is heavier. LO-59 for the mass measurement, LO-56 for the predict-weigh-infer sequence.
Observe how the kitchen is organised and propose a BETTER sorting. LO-55 for the grouping principle, LO-64 because proposing an improved scheme is creativity in planning.
Why shop and home containers are usually transparent. A property put to work in daily life, LO-62.
True/false across opacity, lustre, solubility and what counts as matter, with corrections. Runs the whole LO-55 property-class set at once.
Which chair material best meets hardness, light weight, warmth and cleanability. Selecting materials against four stated requirements, LO-62.

Choose container materials for food waste, broken glass and wastepaper, and say which properties matter. LO-62 for the material choice, LO-63 because separated waste collection is the environmental practice LO-63 covers.
Air is transparent, a wooden door is opaque. LO-55 names transparent, translucent and opaque as its own classes.
Mystery X is rigid and dissolves, Y deforms and does not. Identifies each by placing it on two LO-55 property axes, hardness and solubility.

'Who am I?' from lustre, compressibility, solubility, opacity and having mass without being seen. Identification from observable features, LO-53. The stem is mangled: the five sub-items have been folded into MCQ options with one key.
Build two soluble pairs and two insoluble pairs from vinegar, honey, oil, water, glucose and flour. Soluble/insoluble sorting, LO-55's own example, and notably not restricted to water as the solvent.
What a material is -- any substance used to make an object. The basic identification the chapter rests on, LO-53.
The Rasaratnasamuchchaya's clay and iron crucible. A historical material choice made for a purpose, LO-62.
The conclusion that objects are made of various materials. Identification of materials, LO-53.
What classification is -- grouping by common properties. LO-55's own definition.

Harappan pottery with black designs on red surfaces. A history-of-technology item; LO-61 would require the student to build something, so this is cited at the goal about making things from available materials.
Material choice follows from its properties and the object's purpose. The principle behind LO-62.
Why cloth cannot hold water -- because it is POROUS. Here the item marks the cause, unlike the short-answer version which asked which material to pick instead.
How freshly cut wood looks different from iron. A differentiation of two materials by appearance, LO-54.
Shiny-surfaced materials are lustrous. Naming an observable feature, LO-53.
Paper as the non-lustrous one. Placing a material in the non-lustrous class, LO-55.
Why metals dull over time -- air and moisture act on the surface. A phenomenon related to its cause, LO-57.
Soft materials are those compressed or scratched easily. Defining a property class, LO-55.
The main DIFFERENCE between transparent and opaque materials. The verb makes it LO-54, where item 30's definition of translucency is LO-55.
What translucent materials are. Defining one of LO-55's three optical classes.
Wood as the opaque example. Placing a material in an LO-55 class.
Wall, tree, frosted glass and clear window sorted into opaque, translucent and transparent. Three LO-55 classes applied at once.
What soluble materials do in water. Defining the soluble class, LO-55's own example.
Materials that never dissolve are insoluble. The complementary LO-55 class.
Sugar and salt dissolving to make shikanji. Solubility met in a household task, LO-62.
Sand settles because it is insoluble. Applying the LO-55 solubility class to a prediction.
Heavier means more mass. Naming the physical quantity, LO-59.
Volume is the space occupied. Naming the physical quantity, LO-59.
Mass is measured in grams and kilograms. A physical quantity expressed in SI units, LO-59 -- this chapter's clearest claim on that outcome.
All matter has mass and volume. The two measurable quantities that define matter, LO-59.
Assertion-reason where transparency and hardness are TRUE but not why glass holds water -- non-porosity is. The item marks a correct causal attribution, LO-57.
Which properties can be used to group materials -- lustre, hardness and transparency all qualify. LO-55's criteria. The stem preserves only the last of the three numbered statements.
Three same-size balls bounce differently, so materials differ in property. The lesson is the property difference, LO-54; item 4 was the doing, which is LO-56.
Terra-cotta is baked clay. Naming a material, LO-53.
Why paper will not serve for cooking utensils. Rejecting a material against the demands of a use, LO-62.
Easily compressed or scratched means soft. Defining a property class, LO-55.
Air as the transparent one. Placing a material in an LO-55 optical class.
Lustrous against non-lustrous, shiny against dull. An explicit differentiation, LO-54.
Electrical conductivity is not among the chapter's classifying properties. Tests the boundary of LO-55's criteria set.
A shopkeeper grouping spices apart from pulses is applying classification. The principle at work outside the lab, LO-55.
Assertion-reason: metals dull BECAUSE air and moisture react with the surface. The causal link is the marked part, LO-57.
Material selection turns on properties and purpose, not merely on being cheapest. LO-62's principle. The stem retains only one of the three numbered statements.
Transparency is the crucial property for a window pane. Matching a property to a required function, LO-62.
Scratching with a metal key tests hardness. A test performed to establish a property, LO-56.
Why dissolved oxygen matters to aquatic life. A property connected to a consequence for living things, LO-57.
Guna as the twenty properties of matter in ten opposing pairs. A classification framework for materials, LO-55.
The SI unit of volume is the cubic metre. A physical quantity in SI units, LO-59.
How sugar behaves COMPARED TO sand in water. An explicit comparison of two materials, LO-54.
Unglazed clay is unsuitable for holding liquids. Rejecting a material against a required function, LO-62.
A cotton ball as mridu and laghu -- soft and light. Placing an object against two property classes, LO-55. The Ayurveda reference is corrupted to 'Archived' in the stem.
